words: textual evidence; explicit; inference; thorough; quotation; lead-in
notes: Cite strong and thorough evidence for what a story says outright and for what a reader infers. Grade 8 asked for the single piece that most strongly supports a reading; 9-10 adds thorough: several pieces, explicit and inferred, gathered into one reading, each quotation led in and explained. Practised on short stories of 2,000 to 6,000 words (for example Poe, Maupassant, Saki, London) and on the year's play. Grade 9 takes it to two or three well-chosen quotations per claim with the inference said in the student's words, with a teacher model first and an evidence chart that fades by midyear. Grade 10 carries it across a whole novel. Text demand for English 9: anchors in the grades 9-10 band (2012 supplement to Appendix A: about 1050 to 1335 Lexile), most placed in the lower two thirds, with scaffolding at the high end; a poem or play has no usable measure and rests on the qualitative read.

words: theme; central idea; motif; objective summary; develop; refine
notes: State a theme as a full sentence about people or life (never one word) and trace how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details over the course of a text; write an objective summary with no opinion. Grade 8 tied theme to characters, setting and plot; 9-10 asks how the theme emerges and is refined detail by detail, so students mark the first hint, the turn and the closing image. Practised on short stories and on Romeo and Juliet. Grade 9 limit: one theme per text, traced at three to four points, with a summary of about 100 words checked for opinion words. Grade 10 handles two themes in tension across a novel.

words: complex character; motivation; conflicting motives; foil; interaction; advance the plot
notes: Analyze how a character with more than one motive, or motives at war, develops, how they act on other characters and how that moves the plot or builds the theme. Grade 8 asked how a line of dialogue or an incident propels action or reveals character; 9-10 widens to the whole arc of a complex character. Practised on short stories and the play: Juliet, Romeo, Friar Laurence and the Nurse are the year's main case. Grade 9 limit: one complex character at a time, with a two-column motive chart (what they want, what pulls against it) at three scenes. Teacher note: Romeo and Juliet ends in two suicides; the unit names this before reading, treats it as the play's tragedy and not as a choice to admire, and gives the school's support contacts.

words: connotation; figurative meaning; tone; diction; euphemism; oxymoron; imagery
notes: Work out what words mean as used, including figurative and connotative meanings, and say how a word choice sets tone or a sense of time and place. RL.9-10.4 adds to grade 8 the cumulative impact of many choices; grade 9 begins with the single choice and pairs of choices, and grade 10 owns the cumulative case. L.9-10.5 adds the new figures (euphemism, oxymoron; grade 8 had verbal irony and puns) and nuance among words of like meaning; Romeo and Juliet's oxymorons and the short stories' euphemisms are the practice. Practised on poems (sonnets, ballads, public-domain lyric poems of 14 to 40 lines) and on key passages of the year's stories.

words: pacing; flashback; foreshadowing; suspense; tension; parallel plot; frame
notes: Analyze how an author's choices about structure, the order of events and the handling of time (pacing, flashback, foreshadowing, parallel plots) create mystery, tension or surprise. Grade 8 compared the structures of two texts; 9-10 moves inside one text to name the choice and its effect on a reader. Practised on suspense and twist stories of 2,000 to 6,000 words (Poe, Saki, Bierce's flashback story) and on the play's compressed four days. Grade 9 limit: one structural choice and one named effect per analysis; grade 10 weighs several choices across a novel.

words: source material; allusion; retelling; transform; epic; artistic medium
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-classical-learning (Greek myth and epic in the grade 9 world history course)
notes: Trace how a later work draws on and changes older source material, and compare one subject in two artistic mediums. Grade 8 asked how a modern story draws on myth and renders it new; RL.9-10.9 names a specific work and its source, and grade 9 practises on the Odyssey (a public-domain prose translation, books read whole and in large parts) set beside later poems that answer it (for example Tennyson's Ulysses). RL.9-10.7 starts here: Ovid's Icarus story in translation beside Brueghel's painting of the fall of Icarus, asking what each emphasizes or leaves out. Grade 10 owns both, on Shakespeare and his sources.

words: point of view; cultural experience; translation; setting; world literature
notes: Analyze a point of view or cultural experience in a story written outside the United States. Grade 8 asked about differences in point of view between characters and reader; RL.9-10.6 turns to the culture a work comes from and asks for wide reading of world literature. Grade 9 starts with four to six short stories in public-domain translation from several regions (for example Chekhov, Maupassant, Tagore, a story from the Odyssey's world of guest and host), with a short background note before reading only where the text does not supply it. Grade 9 limit: one story at a time; grade 10 compares across works and adds a longer work.

words: drama; act; scene; soliloquy; aside; sonnet; stanza; epic
notes: Read and understand stories, a whole play and poems in the grades 9-10 band, with scaffolding at the high end (the standard's own end-of-grade-9 line). The year's long texts read whole: Romeo and Juliet (every scene, with audio beside the text and the long-sentence routine for verse) and the Odyssey in prose translation in large parts. Reading volume and a log of a long on-topic book each unit sit here. Text demand for English 9: anchors in the grades 9-10 band (2012 supplement to Appendix A: about 1050 to 1335 Lexile), most placed in the lower two thirds, with scaffolding at the high end; a poem or play has no usable measure and rests on the qualitative read. Grade 10 removes the scaffolding: independent at the high end.

words: central idea; objective summary; literary nonfiction; refine; textual evidence
notes: Cite thorough evidence from nonfiction, find a central idea and show how it emerges and is refined by specific details, and summarize objectively. Grade 8 related the central idea to supporting ideas; 9-10 asks how it is shaped and refined as the text goes. Practised on literary nonfiction of 1,000 to 4,000 words tied to the year's topic sets: essays and memoir passages on journeys and exile beside the Odyssey, and essays on science and risk. RI.9-10.10 here: proficient with scaffolding at the high end. Text demand for English 9: anchors in the grades 9-10 band (2012 supplement to Appendix A: about 1050 to 1335 Lexile), most placed in the lower two thirds, with scaffolding at the high end; a poem or play has no usable measure and rests on the qualitative read.

words: sequence of ideas; connection; distinction; transition; section; technical term
cross_subject: science:HS-LS4-1 (reading an explanation of the evidence for common ancestry in grade 9 biology)
notes: Analyze how an author unfolds a series of ideas or events (the order of points, how each is introduced and developed, the connections drawn) and how particular sentences and paragraphs develop a claim. Grade 8 looked at the role of sentences in one paragraph; RI.9-10.5 widens to larger portions (a section or chapter) and RI.9-10.3 to the whole line of an analysis. RI.9-10.4 starts with technical and connotative words in context. Practised on explanatory science and history essays of 1,500 to 3,000 words with headings. Grade 9 limit: a two-level outline of one text's moves; grade 10 compares how two authors order the same material.

words: rhetoric; purpose; audience; occasion; appeal; ethos; pathos; logos; repetition
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-declaration (the Declaration read as a founding document in grade 8)
notes: Determine a speaker's point of view or purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances it. Grade 8 asked how an author answers conflicting viewpoints; 9-10 adds rhetoric as a set of named moves. Introduces the rhetorical situation (speaker, audience, purpose, occasion) and the three appeals as the year's tool. Practised on short speeches of 250 to 2,000 words; grade 9 starts RI.9-10.9 with two seminal U.S. documents read closely, the Gettysburg Address and an excerpt of Washington's Farewell Address, for how they address union. Grade 10 owns the full set across a theme. Grade 9 limit: name the move and its effect on this audience.

words: claim; reason; valid; relevant; sufficient; fallacy; false statement
cross_subject: math:S-ID.C.9 (correlation is not causation, the commonest fallacy in data claims)
notes: Lay out an argument's claims and judge whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence relevant and sufficient; spot false statements and fallacious reasoning. Grade 8 judged soundness and spotted irrelevant evidence; 9-10 adds validity and named fallacies. Grade 9 teaches a short set of fallacies (hasty generalization, false cause, either-or, attack on the person) on op-ed style essays and letters of 600 to 1,500 words, mapped as claim, reasons and evidence. SL.9-10.3 starts on a recorded speech judged the same way. Grade 10 adds the full judgment on longer arguments.

words: medium; account; emphasis; omission; multimedia; credibility
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-graphic-displays (reading maps, charts and timelines as information)
notes: Compare accounts of one subject in different mediums and say which details each emphasizes. Grade 8 weighed the advantages of mediums in general; 9-10 compares named accounts of one subject. Grade 9 practises on a person's life story told in a print memoir passage and in a short documentary or audio piece (public-domain government film or an original Curio Class recording). SL.9-10.2 starts: combine information from a chart, a talk and a text, asking how credible and accurate each is. Grade 10 adds data displays and judged source sets.

words: analytic paragraph; topic sentence; embedded quotation; commentary; on-demand
notes: Write routinely from texts: analytic paragraphs that state a reading, embed evidence and explain it, plus short on-demand responses in one sitting. W.9-10.9a and 9b apply the grade's reading standards; grade 8 named the same habit at grade 8 demand. Grade 9 builds the analytic paragraph (claim, two quotations, commentary longer than the quotations) to fluency, then joins paragraphs into a short essay; the frame fades by the second semester. The daily exit question is part of this row. Grade 10 moves to the full analytic essay, timed and untimed.

words: explain; extended definition; concrete detail; transition; formal style; implication
cross_subject: science:HS-LS2-7 (explaining a human impact on an ecosystem in grade 9 biology)
notes: Write explanatory pieces that make complex ideas clear: introduce the topic, organize to show connections and distinctions, develop with facts, extended definitions and quotations, use varied transitions and precise words, and close by saying why it matters. Grade 8 asked to examine a topic; 9-10 asks to examine complex ideas and adds extended definitions and implications. Grade 9: one process piece (about 800 to 1,200 words) on a topic set from the year's nonfiction, with a model piece and a rubric used all year, plus short explanations. Grade 10 adds graphics and headings by choice and a longer sourced piece.

words: precise claim; counterclaim; rebuttal; cohesion; objective tone; concluding section
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-historical-argument (claims with evidence from sources in grade 9 world history)
notes: Write arguments on texts and issues with a precise claim, reasons, relevant evidence, a counterclaim and a response, cohesive links and a formal, objective tone. Grade 8 acknowledged opposing claims; 9-10 asks the writer to distinguish them and organize the relations among claim, counterclaim, reasons and evidence. Grade 9 takes W.9-10.1a, c, d and e in full and starts 1b with one counterclaim answered fairly; two process arguments a year (a literary argument and an issue argument from a nonfiction set, 800 to 1,200 words) with a model piece. Grade 10 adds several counterclaims weighed by strengths and limits for a named audience.

words: narrator; point of view; pacing; reflection; telling detail; sensory language
notes: Write narratives, real or imagined, that set out a problem or situation, establish a point of view, move smoothly through events, use dialogue, pacing, description and reflection, and close on what was learned or resolved. Grade 8 established context and point of view; 9-10 adds multiple points of view and plot lines and events that build to a coherent whole. Grade 9: one process narrative (a personal narrative or a story that answers the Odyssey or a short story read) of 1,000 to 1,500 words, with one point of view and one plot line, and short scene-writing from the stories' techniques. Grade 10 adds two points of view or plot lines.

words: task; purpose; audience; revise; edit; peer response; publish
notes: Run the writing process: plan, draft, revise, edit, rewrite or try a new approach, keeping task, purpose and audience in view; produce, publish and update typed work. Grade 8 did this 'with some guidance and support from peers and adults'; 9-10 drops that phrase and asks the writer to judge what is most significant to fix. Grade 9 still runs a structured peer response and a named teacher feedback step on every process piece, and students keep a revision log naming the one biggest change. W.9-10.6: typed, shared and updated where devices allow; a room without them hand-writes and publishes on a class wall. Grade 10 makes revision choices independent.

words: research question; advanced search; authoritative; usefulness; paraphrase; plagiarism; works cited
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-inquiry-questions (drafting supporting questions for an inquiry in grade 9)
notes: Run short research projects (three to five days) that answer a question, including a student's own, narrowing or broadening it as sources come in, and combine several sources. Grade 8 ran short projects with several sources and judged credibility; 9-10 adds advanced searches, judging each source's usefulness for this question, integrating quotations selectively and a standard citation format from a style manual (L.9-10.3a starts here). Grade 9: two short projects tied to the year's topic sets, each ending in a cited short paper or talk. Grade 10 adds one sustained project. Choice of style manual: see the lead list.

words: seminar; norm; prepared; build on; clarify; challenge; qualify
notes: Take part in discussions of texts and issues, prepared with marked evidence, building on others and saying one's own view clearly and persuasively. Grade 8 followed rules for discussion; SL.9-10.1b has students set the rules, goals and roles themselves, and 1c and 1d add relating the talk to larger ideas, drawing others in and summarizing agreement and disagreement. Grade 9: a whole-class text discussion at least twice a unit on the anchor, with the class writing its own norms in unit 1 and sentence frames that fade; partner talk daily. Grade 10 runs student-led seminars.

words: line of reasoning; concise; visual aid; formal register; audience
notes: Present findings with evidence so listeners can follow the line of reasoning, use digital media with purpose, and shift into formal English when the task asks. Grade 8 presented claims with eye contact and volume; 9-10 asks for organization and style fitted to purpose and audience, and strategic media. Grade 9: a three to five minute talk from each short research project and a recited or performed passage of the play (practised rereading aloud), with a look-for sheet. Grade 10 adds a longer talk with questions from the audience.

words: phrase; clause; participial phrase; absolute phrase; relative clause; parallel structure
notes: Use the kinds of phrases (noun, verb, adjectival, adverbial, participial, prepositional, absolute) and clauses (independent, dependent; noun, relative, adverbial) to say exactly what is meant and to vary sentences. Grade 8 explained verbals; grade 9 builds participial and absolute phrases from them. Taught by combining sentences from the anchor texts and from students' drafts, never as grammar on its own. Grade 9 takes L.9-10.1b and introduces parallel structure (1a) on lists; grade 10 owns parallel structure in longer sentences and uses both for style.

words: semicolon; conjunctive adverb; independent clause; comma splice; spelling
notes: Use a semicolon, with or without a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore), to join closely related independent clauses, and spell correctly. Grade 8 punctuated pauses and omissions; 9-10 adds the semicolon and the colon. Grade 9 takes L.9-10.2a and 2c, practised in editing students' own drafts and in fixing comma splices; the colon for quotations (2b) belongs to grade 10, where quotations are integrated into analysis. Language Progressive Skills from earlier grades (fragments, run-ons, pronoun agreement) are checked in the same editing step.

words: word family; derivation; etymology; part of speech; verify; general academic word
notes: Work out unknown and multiple-meaning words from context, word changes (analyze, analysis, analytical) and reference works, then check the guess. Grade 8 used Greek and Latin roots; 9-10 adds patterns of word change across parts of speech and etymology in the dictionary. Each unit's word list comes from its texts, mostly general academic words, met before, during and after reading and returned to later. Grade 9 limit: the class learns 10 to 15 words in depth per unit; grade 10 adds the student's own word log for independence (L.9-10.6).

words: textual evidence; thorough; inference; ambiguity; weigh
notes: Owns RL.9-10.1. Cite strong and thorough evidence across a whole novel and a whole play, including where the text leaves things uncertain. Grade 9 gathered two or three quotations per claim in a story, with a chart; grade 10 tracks evidence across chapters, chooses among competing pieces and says why one is stronger, with no chart. Practised on Frankenstein (1818 text, read whole) and Julius Caesar. Text demand for English 10: anchors reach the high end of the grades 9-10 band (about 1185 to 1335 Lexile and the hardest older prose), read independently by year's end; poems and plays rest on the qualitative read.

words: theme; motif; tension; refine; objective summary
notes: Owns RL.9-10.2. Determine themes and analyze in detail how they emerge and are refined across a long text, and write an objective summary of a whole novel or play. Grade 9 traced one theme in a story or the play at a few points; grade 10 follows two themes that pull against each other (creation and responsibility in Frankenstein, honor and ambition in Julius Caesar) through motifs, and summarizes a book-length text in about 200 words.

words: complex character; motivation; foil; interaction; develop; tragic flaw
notes: Owns RL.9-10.3. Analyze how complex characters with conflicting motives develop over a long text, interact and advance the plot or theme. Grade 9 charted one character at a few scenes; grade 10 follows pairs of characters who shape each other (Victor and the creature, Brutus and Cassius) across the whole work. Teacher note: Frankenstein includes murders and deaths of family members, and Julius Caesar an assassination and suicides; name them before reading and treat them through the works' own judgment.

words: cumulative impact; tone; diction; connotation; nuance; euphemism; oxymoron
notes: Owns RL.9-10.4 and L.9-10.5. Analyze the cumulative impact of many word choices on meaning and tone across a passage, a speech or a poem (how the language builds a time and place, a formal or informal tone). Grade 9 named single choices and pairs; grade 10 tracks a pattern of diction through a whole poem or speech and explains its total effect. L.9-10.5: interpret figures of speech in their role in the text, and the nuance between words with like denotations. Practised on Antony's and Brutus's funeral speeches and on a poetry set (public-domain poems, 14 to 60 lines).

words: frame narrative; nested narrator; pacing; parallel plot; manipulate time; effect
notes: Owns RL.9-10.5. Analyze several structural choices working together across a long text and the effects they create. Grade 9 named one choice and one effect in a short story; grade 10 weighs the whole build of a novel (Frankenstein's nested frame narratives, letters and the creature's story inside Victor's) and of a play's acts, with suspense, mystery and surprise each traced to a choice.

words: world literature; cultural experience; point of view; translation; tradition
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-imperialism-impact (stories written under colonial rule, read beside the history)
notes: Owns RL.9-10.6. Analyze a point of view or cultural experience in works from outside the United States, drawing on a wide reading of world literature. Grade 9 read single short stories in translation; grade 10 reads a longer work (for example a Greek tragedy such as Antigone in a public-domain translation) and a set of stories and poems from at least three regions, comparing how each reflects its culture. Teacher note: the range of public-domain translations leans to older European and South Asian work; see the lead list.

words: source material; adaptation; transform; artistic medium; emphasis; absence
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-classical-learning (Roman history and Plutarch in the grade 9 course)
notes: Owns RL.9-10.9 and RL.9-10.7. Analyze how an author draws on and transforms source material in a specific work: Shakespeare's Julius Caesar beside passages of Plutarch's life of Caesar (public-domain translation), what he kept, cut and invented. Grade 9 compared the Odyssey with later poems that answer it; grade 10 compares line by line against a named source. RL.9-10.7: a key scene in two artistic mediums (the assassination in the play and in a nineteenth-century painting, or a staged recording), saying what each emphasizes or leaves out.

words: novel; tragedy; verse; prose; independent reading
notes: Owns RL.9-10.10. By the end of grade 10, read stories, plays and poems at the high end of the 9-10 band independently and proficiently (the standard's own end-of-grade-10 line; grade 9 had scaffolding at the high end). Long texts read whole: Frankenstein and Julius Caesar; supports are thinned through the year so the last unit's anchor is read without the long-sentence routine. Independent reading of a long on-topic book each unit with a log and a conference. Text demand for English 10: anchors reach the high end of the grades 9-10 band (about 1185 to 1335 Lexile and the hardest older prose), read independently by year's end; poems and plays rest on the qualitative read.

words: central idea; refine; objective summary; literary nonfiction; thorough evidence
notes: Owns RI.9-10.1, RI.9-10.2 and RI.9-10.10. Cite thorough evidence, trace a central idea through a long essay or a chapter of nonfiction, and summarize objectively. Grade 9 did this on essays of up to 4,000 words with scaffolding; grade 10 reads longer and denser nonfiction (science writing beside Frankenstein, on making life and its limits; nineteenth-century essays) at the high end of the band independently by year's end. Text demand for English 10: anchors reach the high end of the grades 9-10 band (about 1185 to 1335 Lexile and the hardest older prose), read independently by year's end; poems and plays rest on the qualitative read.

words: line of reasoning; section; refine; connection; order of points
notes: Owns RI.9-10.3 and RI.9-10.5. Analyze how an author orders and develops a series of ideas and how particular sentences, paragraphs and sections develop and refine claims. Grade 9 outlined one text's moves; grade 10 compares how two authors order the same material (two explanations of one scientific discovery, two accounts of one event) and why. Practised on essays and chapters of 2,000 to 5,000 words.

words: technical meaning; connotation; register; cumulative impact; tone
notes: Owns RI.9-10.4. Determine figurative, connotative and technical meanings and analyze the cumulative impact of word choices on meaning and tone, as in how the language of a court opinion differs from a newspaper's. Grade 9 worked out technical words in explanatory essays; grade 10 compares register across texts on one event (a public-domain court opinion or official report beside a news account of it).

words: rhetoric; purpose; audience; appeal; propaganda; rhetorical question; parallelism
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-totalitarian-regimes (propaganda studied in grade 10 world history)
notes: Owns RI.9-10.6. Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances it across a whole speech or essay. Grade 9 named single moves and their effect; grade 10 explains how the moves work together for an audience and judges whether they serve or manipulate the reader, including wartime speeches beside propaganda. Practised on speeches and essays of 1,000 to 4,000 words.

words: seminal document; founding; liberty; address; related theme
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-constitution-text (the founding documents read in grade 8 civics)
notes: Owns RI.9-10.9. Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance and how they address related themes. Grade 9 read two short documents closely for their rhetoric; grade 10 reads a set on one theme (liberty and who it includes: the Declaration of Independence, the Declaration of Sentiments, Douglass's July Fifth speech, Lincoln's Second Inaugural, Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech) and compares how each takes up the theme. Teacher note: Douglass's speech describes slavery's cruelty directly; prepare the class and keep the focus on his argument. The standard's own example of King's letter is not public domain; see the lead list.

words: valid; sufficient; fallacy; exaggerated evidence; distorted evidence; premise
notes: Owns RI.9-10.8 and SL.9-10.3. Delineate and evaluate a full argument: is the reasoning valid, is the evidence relevant and sufficient, where are false statements and fallacies. Grade 9 mapped short op-eds and named four fallacies; grade 10 maps long arguments with several lines of reasoning, adds fallacies of data and authority, and writes a judgment of the whole. SL.9-10.3 owns the same on a speaker: point of view, reasoning, rhetoric, exaggerated or distorted evidence, on recorded public-domain speeches and debates.

words: account; medium; emphasis; credibility; accuracy; data display
cross_subject: math:8.SP.A.1 (reading scatter plots and patterns of association)
notes: Owns RI.9-10.7 and SL.9-10.2. Analyze accounts of one subject in different mediums, deciding which details each emphasizes, and integrate several sources (visual, numeric, spoken) while judging each for credibility and accuracy. Grade 9 compared a print and a filmed life story; grade 10 works a source set of five or more items on one topic (a report, a graph, a recorded talk, a news piece), as the base of the sustained research project.

words: counterclaim; strengths and limitations; audience; cohesion; formal style; qualify
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-historians-interpretations (weighing competing interpretations in grade 10 world history)
notes: Owns W.9-10.1 with all of a to e. Write arguments that develop claims and counterclaims fairly, with evidence for each and their strengths and limits, for an audience whose knowledge and concerns the writer anticipates. Grade 9 answered one counterclaim; grade 10 weighs several and may qualify its own claim, in two process arguments (literary and issue, 1,200 to 1,800 words) and timed arguments. Writing shares across the two years lean toward about 40 percent argument, 40 informative and 20 narrative, the grade 12 shares in the standards' introduction.

words: complex idea; extended definition; formatting; graphic; domain vocabulary; implication
cross_subject: science:HS-ESS3-5 (explaining what climate data and forecasts show, in grade 10 science)
notes: Owns W.9-10.2 with all of a to f. Write explanations of complex ideas with headings, figures or tables where they help, sourced facts and quotations, varied transitions, domain words and a close that draws out implications. Grade 9 wrote a process explanation without graphics; grade 10 writes a longer sourced explanatory piece (1,200 to 1,800 words) with at least one figure or table the writer makes, and short explanations across units.

words: multiple points of view; plot line; pacing; reflection; coherent whole
notes: Owns W.9-10.3 with all of a to e. Write narratives with more than one point of view or plot line, sequenced so events build into a coherent whole, with telling detail and a reflective close. Grade 9 kept one point of view and one line; grade 10 writes one process narrative (for example a story told by two narrators, in answer to Frankenstein's nested tellings, 1,500 to 2,000 words) and narrative passages inside other writing.

words: revise; significant; audience; publish; update; shared document
notes: Owns W.9-10.4, W.9-10.5 and W.9-10.6. Produce clear, coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience and revise independently for what matters most. Grade 9 used a structured peer response and teacher step; grade 10 students set their own revision goal from the rubric and judge their changes, and the teacher step becomes a conference. W.9-10.6: publish and update a shared or linked product (the research project's page or document, with links to sources); the plan says what a room without devices does.

words: sustained research; synthesize; narrow; broaden; usefulness; integrate; works cited
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-research-argument (a researched argument in grade 10 world history)
notes: Owns W.9-10.7 and W.9-10.8. Run short projects and one sustained project (about three weeks) that answers a self-generated question, narrowing or broadening as needed, synthesizing many sources, with advanced searches, a judgment of each source's usefulness, selective quotation and a full citation form. Grade 9 ran two short projects; grade 10 adds the sustained one and synthesis across sources that disagree. Applies L.9-10.3a, following a style manual's format; e10-l-syntax-style owns L.9-10.3.

words: literary analysis; thesis; embedded quotation; commentary; timed writing
notes: Owns W.9-10.9 and W.9-10.10. Draw evidence from literature and nonfiction to support full analytic essays, applying the grade's reading standards (9a, for example Shakespeare's use of Plutarch; 9b, judging an argument), and write routinely over long and short time frames. Grade 9 built the analytic paragraph and a short essay; grade 10 writes the multi-paragraph analytic essay with a thesis, both through the process and in one timed sitting, plus the daily exit question.

words: student-led seminar; consensus; propel; diverse perspectives; qualify; synthesize
notes: Owns SL.9-10.1 with all of a to d. Run student-led discussions: students prepare from texts and research, set their own rules and roles, propel the talk with questions that tie it to larger ideas, bring others in, and summarize agreement and disagreement, qualifying their views. Grade 9 discussions were teacher-led with fading frames; grade 10 hands leading to students, with the teacher observing against a look-for sheet, at least twice a unit on the anchor.

words: line of reasoning; substance; digital media; formal English; audience questions
notes: Owns SL.9-10.4, SL.9-10.5 and SL.9-10.6. Present findings clearly and concisely with a line of reasoning the audience can follow, use digital media strategically, and adapt speech to context. Grade 9 gave short talks from short projects; grade 10 presents the sustained research project (8 to 10 minutes with questions from the audience) and performs a speech from Julius Caesar, judged on the same look-for sheet.

words: parallel structure; phrase; clause; style; register; style manual
notes: Owns L.9-10.1 and L.9-10.3. Use parallel structure (a Language Progressive Skill, checked in later grades too) and the full range of phrases and clauses to convey meaning and add variety, and apply knowledge of language to make choices for meaning or style and to read more fully. Grade 9 built the phrase and clause types; grade 10 studies parallelism in the year's speeches (Lincoln, Antony) and imitates it, and edits to a style manual (L.9-10.3a, applied in research writing). Taught through sentences from the anchors and from drafts.

words: colon; quotation; semicolon; list; spelling
notes: Owns L.9-10.2 with all of a to c. Use a colon to introduce a list or a quotation, keep the semicolon from grade 9 in use, and spell correctly. Grade 9 taught the semicolon; grade 10 adds the colon, practised where it is needed most, in introducing quotations in analytic essays and research writing, and edits drafts for all three.

words: word family; etymology; verify; reference; general academic word; domain word
notes: Owns L.9-10.4 and L.9-10.6. Choose flexibly among context, word changes and reference works to settle a word's meaning, verify it, and gather words independently. Grade 9 taught the strategies on the unit word list; grade 10 has students keep their own log of words important to understanding and use them in writing and talk, on top of a unit list of 10 to 15 words met before, during and after reading and returned to later.
